name: Pelargonium sidoides
short: 34 WHO reports of suspected allergy, 2 treated for circulatory failure. Liver: reports raised concern; 15 reassessed, none probable. Respiratory trials: more adverse events than control, none serious.
text: The WHO international pharmacovigilance programme had received 34 case reports of allergic reactions suspected to be associated with Pelargonium extract (from P. sidoides and P. reniforme roots), all from Germany; in a number of them the timing and description suggested an acute type I hypersensitivity reaction, and two patients needed treatment for circulatory failure. On liver injury, the drug commission of the German medical association interpreted spontaneous reports as showing some hepatotoxic potential of Pelargonium sidoides, but a reassessment of 15 of these cases with a liver-specific causality scale found none with highly probable or probable causality, citing confounding factors such as other final diagnoses and poor data quality, and concluded that convincing evidence that it was a liver toxin was lacking in those cases. A non-interventional post-authorisation study in 300 adults taking it for the common cold found no signs or symptoms of liver toxicity and no serious adverse events after seven days; dizziness, drowsiness, headache and increased appetite were each reported by 1.3% to 2.0%, and the authors asked for caution in interpreting results given the study's limitations. In a Cochrane review of 8 trials in acute respiratory infections, adverse events were more common with Pelargonium sidoides than with control, but none were serious; the abstract does not say which events these were. The allergy report notes a theoretical risk of interactions with anticoagulants such as warfarin and with antiplatelet drugs such as aspirin; no clinical interaction data were found in the cited sources.
